opus-5.5.text:
I think generation is often misunderstood in this discussion. Many people equate a world model with a video generation model: if you can produce a realistic video of the future, you must understand the world. I don't think that's quite right.

Generation is a very useful training signal. Asking a model to predict the next frame, or the next state, forces it to absorb a lot of structure: physics, object permanence, cause and effect. In that sense generation works like next-token prediction in language. It's a powerful self-supervised objective that lets you use enormous amounts of data without labels.

But generation is a means, not the goal. The purpose of a world model is to support decisions. An agent needs to ask, "If I take this action, what happens?", and then use the answer to plan. For that, you don't need every pixel to be correct. You need the parts that matter for the task to be correct. A model can produce beautiful videos and still get the causal consequence of an action wrong. Another model can be blurry and ugly visually and still be very useful for control.

So I see two levels. At the pixel level, generation is a good way to learn representations and to check whether the model has absorbed the data distribution. At the abstract level, the model should predict in a latent space that captures what's relevant for reasoning and action. I suspect the most effective systems will combine the two. They'll use generation heavily during learning, but the actual "thinking" and planning will happen on more compact representations.

There's also a connection to what we've seen in language models. In language, understanding and generation turned out to be unified, because the output space, text, is already abstract and compressed. In vision and the physical world, the raw signal is extremely redundant, so pure generation spends a lot of capacity on details that don't matter. One open question for the field is how to get the same "understanding emerges from generation" effect in vision without wasting all that capacity on texture and lighting. I don't think anyone has fully solved that yet. That's why I'm cautious about saying that generation alone gives you a world model, even though I think it's an indispensable part of the recipe.

r001.rationale: The response calls generation a means rather than the goal and says generation alone may not produce a world model, but it does not state that understanding can occur without generation.

r002.rationale: It says self-supervised generation can use enormous amounts of unlabeled data, but does not identify ease of obtaining training data as the reason to favor it.

r003.rationale: The response says generation is an “indispensable part of the recipe” and that effective systems will use it heavily during learning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think generation is often misunderstood as the goal of a world model, when really it's closer to a tool, or maybe a byproduct. The real purpose of a world model is to let an agent predict and understand how the world changes in response to its actions, and then plan on top of that. Whether it can render a beautiful pixel-perfect video is secondary.

That said, I don't think generation is useless. For a long time my view was that in computer vision, understanding and generation were somewhat separate tracks. Classification, detection, segmentation were about compressing the world into labels. Generation was about producing pixels. But in the past few years it has become clear they are deeply connected. If you can generate the next frame correctly, that means you have internalized something about physics, about object permanence, about causality. Generation becomes a very strict supervision signal, because the world doesn't give you labels, but it does give you the next moment.

So I would frame it like this. Generation is the training objective, or at least one of the most natural ones, because it forces the model to account for everything rather than only the parts a human bothered to annotate. But the thing we actually care about is the latent representation that emerges, the internal state that captures dynamics. In an ideal world model, you might never decode back to pixels at inference time. You would plan entirely in that latent space, and only generate when you need to inspect what the model is imagining, or to communicate with humans.

There's also a tension here that I think is worth being honest about. Pixel-level generation spends enormous capacity on details that are irrelevant for decision making, like the texture of a wall or the exact shape of a cloud. A model that spends most of its parameters getting those right may actually be worse at the things that matter, like whether a cup will fall when pushed. So the research question I find most interesting is how to keep the rigor of a generative objective while letting the model decide what deserves to be modeled precisely and what can be abstracted away.

If I had to summarize, I'd say generation is how a world model learns to see, but it isn't what a world model is for.

r001.rationale: The response calls generation a tool and says pixel rendering is secondary, but it does not clearly state that understanding can occur without generation. It also says generation is how a world model learns to see.

r002.rationale: It favors generation as supervision because the world provides the next moment even when human labels are unavailable, communicating the accessibility of that training signal.

r003.rationale: It describes generation as a training objective, but does not state that current methods still depend on generative training.

astra-6.text:
I see generation as a way for a world model to express what it thinks could happen. Given the current situation, and perhaps an action, can it generate a plausible next state or a possible future?

But generating something that looks convincing is only part of the problem. For a world model, the generated future needs to be consistent with the dynamics of the world. If I change an action, the consequences should change appropriately. And when the outcome is uncertain, the model should be able to represent multiple possibilities.

So generation becomes useful for prediction and planning. You can imagine taking different actions, compare the possible outcomes, and then decide what to do. The key question is whether those imagined outcomes are reliable enough to guide action.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generation as expressing possible futures and supporting planning, but does not state that understanding can occur without generation.

r002.rationale: It gives no reason based on training data availability for favoring generative supervision or self-supervision.

r003.rationale: It describes generation for prediction and planning, but makes no claim about current world-model training depending on generative training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generation is a way for a world model to express what it believes could happen. Given what it has observed, and perhaps an action, can it generate a plausible next state? That makes generation useful for prediction, simulation, and planning.

But generating something that looks realistic is only part of the problem. A model can produce convincing images or video without reliably understanding how actions change the world. For a world model, I care about whether the generated outcomes stay consistent with the underlying dynamics, and whether the model can represent uncertainty when several outcomes are possible.

So I see generation as an important capability, but the goal is broader: to build a model that lets an agent imagine consequences and use those imagined consequences to make better decisions. That generation might happen in pixels, or it might happen in a more compact internal representation.

r001.rationale: The response calls generation an important capability but does not state that understanding can exist without generation.

r002.rationale: It gives prediction, simulation, and planning as uses of generation, but does not cite ease of obtaining training data as a reason to favor generative supervision.

r003.rationale: It does not say that current world-model training depends on generative training.
